symptoms: persistent sadness or emptiness for more than 2 weeks
loss of interest or pleasure in activities
significant weight loss/gain or appetite change
feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt
diminished ability to think or concentrate
recurrent thoughts of death or suicide
guidance: Depression is a medical illness, not a weakness. Effective treatments include cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), interpersonal therapy, and antidepressant medications (SSRIs, SNRIs). Free mental health care is available at government hospitals and District Mental Health Program (DMHP) centers. iCall helpline: 9152987821. If suicidal, seek emergency care.

symptoms: depressed mood for most of the day, for at least 2 years
guidance: Dysthymia is a chronic but less severe form of depression. It often responds to psychotherapy (CBT) and antidepressants. The DMHP provides free counseling. Long-term management improves quality of life.
precautions: Monitor for episodes of major depression

symptoms: manic episodes lasting at least 7 days (elevated mood, grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsivity, risky behavior)
depressive episodes (low mood, fatigue, suicidal thoughts)
guidance: Bipolar I requires lifelong mood stabilizers (lithium, valproate, lamotrigine). Antipsychotics for acute mania. Never stop medication abruptly. Maintain a regular sleep-wake cycle. Free treatment is available at government psychiatric centers. Family support is crucial.
precautions: Watch for early warning signs of relapse

symptoms: hypomanic episodes (less severe than mania, lasting at least 4 days)
guidance: Mood stabilizers (lamotrigine, lithium) and sometimes antidepressants with caution. Psychotherapy (CBT, psychoeducation) helps prevent relapse. Regular monitoring is essential.
precautions: Do not take antidepressants alone without mood stabilizer

symptoms: chronic fluctuating mood with mild hypomanic and depressive symptoms for at least 2 years
never meet full criteria for major depression or mania
guidance: May progress to bipolar disorder. Treatment includes mood stabilizers and psychotherapy. Psychoeducation helps cope with mood swings.

symptoms: excessive worry about various events or activities (e.g., work, health)
guidance: GAD is very treatable with CBT, relaxation techniques, and SSRIs/SNRIs. Mindfulness and deep breathing are helpful. Avoid caffeine and alcohol. Free counseling at DMHP.

symptoms: recurrent unexpected panic attacks (sudden intense fear, palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, fear of dying)
guidance: Panic disorder is treatable with CBT (exposure, cognitive restructuring) and SSRIs. During an attack, practice slow breathing and grounding (5-4-3-2-1). Avoid avoidance behaviors. Free treatment available.
precautions: Do not fear the fear itself

symptoms: marked fear of social situations where one may be scrutinized
guidance: CBT (exposure therapy and social skills training) is highly effective. SSRIs are helpful. Support groups and gradual exposure reduce symptoms.

symptoms: marked fear of a specific object or situation (e.g., heights, animals, needles, flying)
avoidance or endurance with intense distress
guidance: Exposure therapy (gradual, systematic desensitization) is the gold standard. CBT and relaxation techniques. Virtual reality therapy is also effective.
precautions: Avoidance reinforces fear – gradual exposure is key
Do not force confrontation without support

symptoms: anxiety about places where escape might be difficult or help unavailable
typically fear of open spaces, crowds, public transport
avoidance leading to confinement to home
guidance: CBT with exposure and response prevention. SSRIs may help. Gradually increase activities outside. Supportive therapy.

symptoms: recurrent obsessions (intrusive thoughts, images, urges) causing anxiety
compulsions (repetitive behaviors or mental acts) to reduce anxiety
e.g., excessive cleaning, checking, counting, ordering
insight may be good or poor
guidance: Gold-standard: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) therapy. SSRIs (clomipramine, fluoxetine) also effective. Do not accommodate rituals. Free treatment at DMHP.
precautions: Do not perform rituals to reduce anxiety in therapy – it prevents progress
Do not give in to compulsions
Family should not participate in rituals

symptoms: exposure to traumatic event (actual or threatened death, serious injury, sexual violence)
negative alterations in mood and cognition
guidance: Trauma-focused CBT, EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) are effective. SSRIs help. Seek specialized trauma services. Government hospitals offer care.
precautions: Do not avoid all reminders – therapy helps process

symptoms: similar to PTSD but occurs within 1 month of trauma
guidance: Early intervention can prevent PTSD. Provide psychological first aid, trauma-focused CBT. Most recover with supportive care.

symptoms: emotional or behavioral symptoms within 3 months of a stressful event (e.g., divorce, job loss, illness)
not meeting criteria for other disorders
guidance: Brief therapy (CBT) and problem-solving counseling. Usually resolves once stressor ends or coping improves. Free counseling available.

symptoms: negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition, alogia, anhedonia, asociality)
onset usually in late adolescence to early adulthood
guidance: Antipsychotic medications (risperidone, olanzapine, haloperidol) are the mainstay – available free at government hospitals. Adherence is crucial. Psychosocial rehabilitation (occupational therapy, social skills training). Family psychoeducation. Never stop medication abruptly.
precautions: Medication adherence is critical to prevent relapse
Monitor side effects (weight gain, metabolic syndrome)

symptoms: features of schizophrenia (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech) and mood episode (mania or depression) occurring together
psychotic symptoms occur without mood episodes as well
guidance: Treatment combines antipsychotics and mood stabilizers/antidepressants. Long-term management is essential. Psychotherapy and vocational support.

symptoms: non-bizarre delusions (e.g., being followed, poisoned, loved) for at least 1 month
functioning relatively normal except for delusional content
guidance: Antipsychotics (pimozide, risperidone) may help. CBT for delusions. Insight is often poor – therapeutic alliance is key.
precautions: Do not argue with delusions – validate feelings

symptoms: sudden onset of psychotic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech) lasting 1 day to 1 month
guidance: Antipsychotics and supportive care. Usually good prognosis. Rule out substance-induced or organic causes.

symptoms: delusions develop in a person in close relationship with someone who already has a delusion
the delusion resolves when they are separated
guidance: Separate the individuals, treat the primary case with antipsychotics, and provide therapy to the secondary.

symptoms: can occur in schizophrenia, mood disorders, or medical conditions
guidance: Catatonia is a medical emergency – treat with benzodiazepines (lorazepam) and ECT. Rule out underlying medical causes (encephalitis, metabolic).

symptoms: restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight
denial of seriousness of low weight
guidance: Multidisciplinary: medical, nutritional, and psychological (CBT, family-based therapy). Hospitalization if severe weight loss or electrolyte imbalance. Eating disorders have the highest mortality among mental illnesses.
precautions: Do not focus on weight in conversations

symptoms: recurrent episodes of binge eating (large amount of food in short time with loss of control)
compensatory behaviors (vomiting, laxatives, fasting, excessive exercise)
self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape/weight
occurs at least once a week for 3 months
guidance: CBT (CBT-E) is first-line. SSRIs (fluoxetine) reduce binge-purge cycles. Nutritional counseling. Address dental erosion and electrolyte imbalances.

symptoms: recurrent episodes of binge eating without compensatory behaviors
eating rapidly, until uncomfortably full, alone due to embarrassment
occurs at least once a week for 3 months
guidance: CBT, interpersonal therapy, and medications (lisdexamfetamine, SSRIs) are effective. Weight management and self-help support.

symptoms: persistent eating of non-nutritive substances (e.g., dirt, chalk, soap) for at least 1 month
guidance: Check for nutritional deficiencies (iron, zinc). Behavioral interventions. Address underlying mental health issues.

symptoms: repeated regurgitation of food over at least 1 month
may be re-chewed, re-swallowed, or spit out
occurs in both children and adults
guidance: Behavioral therapy (diaphragmatic breathing, habit reversal). Address comorbid anxiety. Medical evaluation for weight loss.

symptoms: difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or early morning awakening
occurs at least 3 nights per week for ≥3 months
guidance: Cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment. Sleep hygiene: regular schedule, no screens before bed, avoid caffeine/alcohol. Medications (temporary) as needed.

symptoms: excessive daytime sleepiness despite ≥7 hours of sleep
not better explained by other conditions
guidance: Rule out sleep apnea, narcolepsy, or medical causes. Treatment: stimulants (modafinil), lifestyle changes, good sleep hygiene.

symptoms: cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions)
guidance: Stimulants (modafinil, methylphenidate) for sleepiness; antidepressants for cataplexy. Scheduled naps help. Sodium oxybate for severe cases. Neurologist referral.

symptoms: urge to move legs, often accompanied by uncomfortable sensations
worse at rest, relieved by movement
guidance: Check ferritin (treat if low). Medications: dopamine agonists (pramipexole), gabapentin. Avoid caffeine, alcohol. Iron supplementation if deficient.

symptoms: repeated nightmares (vivid, dysphoric dreams) leading to awakenings
not due to substance or other disorder
guidance: Image rehearsal therapy (IRT) is effective. Treat PTSD if present. Good sleep hygiene.

symptoms: arising from sleep and walking, with blank stare, unresponsive, confused
occurs in deep sleep, usually first third of night
guidance: Safety measures: lock windows, remove obstacles. Avoid sleep deprivation. Usually benign. Address underlying stress.
precautions: Do not wake abruptly (may cause agitation)

symptoms: sudden arousal from sleep with screaming, intense fear
occurs in non-REM sleep, often in children
guidance: Reassure; most resolve with age. Safety measures. Identify and reduce stress. In adults, consider psychiatric evaluation.

Medically supervised detoxification (benzodiazepines) for withdrawal. Naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram to reduce cravings. Psychosocial therapy (CBT, motivational interviewing). Support groups (AA). Free de-addiction centers at government hospitals.
precautions: Do not stop abruptly without medical supervision (seizure risk)

guidance: Medication-assisted treatment (MAT) with buprenorphine/naloxone or methadone is first-line. Detoxification alone leads to high relapse. Counseling and social support are crucial. Free services at government de-addiction centers.
CBT and motivational enhancement therapy. Address underlying anxiety/depression. No specific medication currently approved.

symptoms: strong craving, loss of control, tolerance, withdrawal (depression, fatigue, sleep changes)
guidance: CBT, contingency management. No specific pharmacotherapy. Supportive treatment. Address medical complications (cardiovascular).

symptoms: use of inhalants (glue, paint thinner, aerosols)
guidance: CBT, motivational interviewing. Address medical complications (hepatic, renal, neurological). Liver transplant may be needed in severe cases.
Nicotine replacement therapy (gum, patches) and medications (bupropion, varenicline) double quit rates. Counseling and support groups. Free services at government health centers.

symptoms: need to gamble with increasing amounts
guidance: CBT, motivational interviewing, and support groups (Gamblers Anonymous). Address co-occurring depression or substance use.

symptoms: loss of interest in other activities
guidance: CBT, family therapy, and digital detox strategies. Set time limits and promote alternative activities.
Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) is the gold standard. Mentalization-based therapy and transference-focused therapy. Medications for co-occurring depression/anxiety. Crisis management is essential.

symptoms: disregard for and violation of others' rights
guidance: Cognitive-behavioral approaches, contingency management. Limited treatment effectiveness; focus on harm reduction and legal consequences. Comorbid substance use should be treated.

symptoms: need to be center of attention
guidance: Psychodynamic therapy, CBT. Help develop more stable sense of self and deeper relationships.
Psychotherapy (psychodynamic, CBT) can help improve empathy and self-reflection. Focus on realistic self-appraisal and interpersonal functioning.
CBT (social skills training, gradual exposure) is effective. Build self-esteem. May respond to SSRIs for anxiety.

symptoms: excessive need to be taken care of
guidance: CBT to build autonomy and decision-making skills. Assertiveness training. Address anxiety. Gradually reduce reliance.

symptoms: preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and control
devotion to work to the exclusion of leisure
guidance: Psychotherapy (CBT) to reduce rigidity and improve flexibility. Address underlying anxiety. Different from OCD – no compulsive rituals.

symptoms: presence of two or more distinct identity states
recurrent gaps in memory for everyday events
guidance: Long-term psychotherapy (specialized) focusing on integration and trauma processing. Grounding techniques. Avoid hypnosis without expertise.

symptoms: inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually traumatic or stressful
guidance: Psychotherapy to safely recover memories. Grounding and stabilization. Rule out organic causes.

symptoms: persistent or recurrent experiences of unreality (detachment from self or surroundings)
guidance: CBT, grounding techniques, mindfulness. SSRIs may help comorbid anxiety. Rule out substance-induced.

symptoms: one or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or cause disruption
excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to symptoms
guidance: CBT, mindfulness, and reassurance. Address underlying stress. Avoid unnecessary medical tests. Regular follow-up with a trusted physician.
precautions: Validate symptoms but focus on function

symptoms: preoccupation with having a serious illness
guidance: CBT is effective. Reduce checking and reassurance. Build tolerance to uncertainty. Rule out organic causes once.

symptoms: symptoms of altered voluntary motor or sensory function (e.g., paralysis, seizures, blindness, numbness)
guidance: Multidisciplinary: neurology and psychiatry. CBT, physical therapy, and treatment of underlying psychological stressors. Avoid iatrogenic harm.
precautions: Neurological evaluation to rule out organic

symptoms: falsification of physical or psychological symptoms, without external reward
deceptive behavior even in the absence of obvious benefit
may present with dramatic, inconsistent symptoms
guidance: Difficult to treat – establish a therapeutic alliance, avoid confrontation. Address underlying personality issues. Protect from unnecessary procedures.

symptoms: intentional production of false or grossly exaggerated symptoms for external gain (e.g., avoiding work, financial compensation)
not a mental disorder but a condition
guidance: Identify through inconsistency and motivation. Address with a non-judgmental approach. Offer appropriate referral.
precautions: Offer treatment if actual disorder present

category: Male Sexual Dysfunction (Erectile Dysfunction, Premature Ejaculation)
symptoms: may be associated with anxiety or physical illness
guidance: Medical evaluation (vascular, hormonal, neurological). Treat underlying conditions. Psychological counseling, CBT, and pharmacotherapy (PDE5 inhibitors, SSRIs for premature ejaculation).

category: Female Sexual Dysfunction (Arousal, Orgasmic, Pain Disorders)
guidance: Biopsychosocial approach. Rule out medical causes (hormonal, pelvic). Psychotherapy (CBT, sex therapy) and pelvic floor physiotherapy. Address relationship issues.

symptoms: marked incongruence between experienced/expressed gender and assigned gender
strong desire to be of the other gender
guidance: Psychotherapy (supportive), hormonal therapy (cross-sex hormones), and surgical interventions (gender-affirming surgeries) for eligible individuals. Multidisciplinary care. Respect identity.

symptoms: sexual arousal to atypical objects/situations, causing distress or impairment, or involving non-consenting persons
guidance: Treatment: cognitive-behavioral therapy, relapse prevention, and sometimes antiandrogens or SSRIs to reduce sexual drive. Legal and ethical considerations. Protect potential victims.

symptoms: recurrent behavioral outbursts representing a failure to control aggressive impulses
guidance: CBT, anger management, and SSRIs or mood stabilizers. Identify triggers and develop coping strategies.

symptoms: no other motive (e.g., financial gain, revenge)
guidance: CBT and medication (SSRIs). Address impulsivity. Safety supervision. Monitor for comorbid conduct disorder.

symptoms: recurrent failure to resist impulses to steal objects not needed for personal use
tension before and relief after stealing
guidance: CBT, impulse control training, and SSRIs. Address legal consequences. Therapy focuses on urge surfing.

symptoms: recurrent pulling out of one's hair leading to hair loss
guidance: Habit reversal therapy (HRT) is the most effective. CBT and acceptance-based therapy. Medications (SSRIs, N-acetylcysteine) may help.

symptoms: recurrent skin picking resulting in lesions
guidance: Habit reversal training, CBT, and SSRIs. Keep nails short, cover picking areas, and use fidget objects.

symptoms: preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in appearance that are not observable or slight
repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, excessive grooming, seeking reassurance)
guidance: CBT (especially exposure and response prevention) and SSRIs. Avoid unnecessary cosmetic procedures. Address distorted body image.

symptoms: persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of value
accumulation leading to clutter that compromises living areas
guidance: CBT (specialized for hoarding), motivational interviewing, and sometimes SSRIs. Practical help with decluttering and decision-making.

symptoms: acute onset of confusion, inattention, disorganized thinking, altered consciousness
may have hallucinations, delusions, agitation, or lethargy
often due to medical condition, substance, or medication
guidance: Medical emergency – identify and treat underlying cause. Environmental measures (reorientation, familiar objects, calm setting). Antipsychotics (haloperidol) for agitation if needed.

symptoms: gradual memory loss affecting daily life
guidance: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) and memantine. Supportive care, environmental modifications, and caregiver education. Free memory clinics at some government hospitals.
Control vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, cholesterol). Medications similar to Alzheimer's. Rehabilitation and lifestyle changes.

symptoms: personality and behavior changes (apathy, disinhibition, loss of empathy)
relatively preserved memory in early stages
guidance: Supportive care, behavioral interventions, speech therapy. No cure. Genetic counseling if familial.
Cholinesterase inhibitors may help; avoid antipsychotics (can worsen). Management of motor and autonomic symptoms.
Treat depression with SSRIs. Psychosis: clozapine or quetiapine (avoid typical antipsychotics). Optimize dopaminergic therapy. Multidisciplinary care.
Genetic counseling. Symptomatic: tetrabenazine for chorea, antidepressants, antipsychotics. Multidisciplinary care. Prognosis: 15-20 years after onset.

symptoms: multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic
guidance: Psychoeducation, behavioral therapy (habit reversal), and medications (antipsychotics, alpha-agonists). Supportive school environment.

category: Chronic Motor or Vocal Tic Disorder
symptoms: single or multiple motor or vocal tics, but not both
present for more than a year
not due to substance or other condition
guidance: Similar to Tourette's – behavioral therapy, medication if needed. Usually mild and manageable.
CBT and supportive therapy. Low-dose antipsychotics may help. Focus on social skills.
Supportive therapy, social skills training. Respect need for distance. Focus on functional goals.

symptoms: pervasive distrust and suspiciousness of others
guidance: Difficult to treat due to distrust. Build therapeutic alliance slowly. CBT to challenge assumptions. Address hypervigilance.

symptoms: eating or feeding disturbance leading to significant weight loss, nutritional deficiency, or dependence on supplements
avoidance based on sensory characteristics or fear of adverse consequences
guidance: Nutritional rehabilitation and CBT. Address sensory issues and anxiety. Family-based therapy for children.
Treat obstructive sleep apnea with CPAP. Address depression/anxiety. Weight loss. Avoid sedatives.

symptoms: persistent sleep-wake schedule misalignment with the environment
e.g., delayed sleep phase, shift work disorder
guidance: Chronotherapy, light therapy, melatonin, and sleep hygiene. For shift work, strategic napping and caffeine.

symptoms: repeated involuntary urination during sleep in adults
often associated with stress or anxiety
guidance: Rule out UTI, diabetes, neurologic. Behavioral: fluid restriction, bladder training. Desmopressin or alarm therapy if indicated.

symptoms: repeated passage of feces into inappropriate places (e.g., underwear) in adults
may be associated with stress or trauma
guidance: Rule out organic causes. Behavioral therapy, bowel training, and treatment of underlying psychological issues.

symptoms: marked delay or absence of ejaculation
guidance: Address anxiety, relationship issues. Medications (e.g., oxytocin) may help. Sex therapy.

symptoms: marked delay or absence of orgasm
guidance: Sex therapy, sensate focus exercises, and CBT. Address relationship issues. Vibratory stimulation may help.
Pelvic floor physiotherapy, vaginal dilators, and CBT. Address anxiety. Gradually desensitize.

symptoms: craving, tolerance, withdrawal (anxiety, insomnia, seizures, tremor)
guidance: Gradual taper (as long-term benzodiazepines) under medical supervision. CBT and supportive therapy. Flumazenil in overdose.

category: Sedative, Hypnotic, or Anxiolytic Use Disorder
symptoms: use of barbiturates or other sedatives
guidance: Medically supervised detoxification. Long-term therapy for underlying issues. Relapse prevention.

symptoms: use of LSD, psilocybin, ketamine, etc.
guidance: CBT, motivational interviewing. Address psychosis if present. No specific pharmacotherapy.
Gradual reduction. Manage withdrawal symptoms. Substitute with decaf.

symptoms: use of anabolic steroids despite adverse effects (aggression, mood swings, liver toxicity)
guidance: Psychotherapy, harm reduction, and medical monitoring for organ damage. Address body image issues.

symptoms: lies are often extravagant and not self-serving
may be associated with personality disorders
guidance: Psychotherapy to address underlying issues. Establish trust. Cognitive restructuring.

symptoms: failure to resist impulses that harm self or others
e.g., sexual impulses, reckless driving, fire-setting
increasing tension before act, relief after
guidance: CBT, contingency management, and medication (SSRIs, mood stabilizers). Address triggers.

symptoms: deliberate self-inflicted damage to body tissue (cutting, burning, scratching) without suicidal intent
often to relieve tension or regulate emotions
may be associated with BPD or PTSD
guidance: DBT is the most effective. Address underlying emotional dysregulation. Crisis plan. Keep sharp objects secured.

symptoms: involuntary trance states with narrowing of awareness, often in cultural or religious contexts
not considered pathological in cultural context unless distressing
guidance: Cultural understanding. If distressing, psychotherapy. Rule out epilepsy or psychosis.

symptoms: intense, persistent longing for the deceased
frequent intrusive memories, difficulty accepting death
guidance: Grief-focused CBT and complicated grief therapy. Support groups. Medications for associated depression.

symptoms: episodes resembling epileptic seizures but with no epileptiform activity on EEG
often associated with emotional distress or trauma
may have pelvic thrusting, asynchronous movements, crying
guidance: Diagnosis by video-EEG. CBT and trauma-focused therapy. Avoid antiepileptic drugs. Validate the reality of the experience.

category: Factitious Disorder Imposed on Another (Munchausen by Proxy)
symptoms: caregiver falsifies or induces illness in a person under their care (usually a child)
guidance: Protect the victim. Remove from the caregiver if needed. Psychiatric treatment for the perpetrator. Legal involvement.

symptoms: may be associated with depression or anxiety
guidance: Couples or family therapy. Communication skills training. Mediation if needed.
Rest, stress management, therapy (CBT), and organizational changes. Set work-life boundaries. Engage in leisure activities.

symptoms: excessive worry about exams or grades
guidance: Time management, relaxation techniques, study skills training, and counseling. Address perfectionism.
CBT (exposure, cognitive restructuring) and relaxation training. Study skills and test-taking strategies.
Cognitive restructuring, media literacy, and building self-esteem. Address eating disorder if present.

symptoms: depression or mania directly caused by substance intoxication or withdrawal
guidance: Substance cessation. Treat the underlying substance use. Mood symptoms usually improve with abstinence.

symptoms: hallucinations or delusions due to substance use (e.g., cannabis, amphetamines)
guidance: Substance cessation. Short-term antipsychotics if needed. Monitor for persistence.

symptoms: anxiety, panic, or phobic symptoms due to substance (e.g., caffeine, cannabis, withdrawal from alcohol)
guidance: Identify and stop substance. Behavioral management. Short-term benzodiazepines may be used but avoid if possible.

symptoms: symptoms resembling OCD but not meeting full criteria
e.g., compulsive checking, ordering, or collecting
guidance: CBT, ERP, and SSRIs. Address distress.

symptoms: multiple, recurrent, often changing somatic symptoms over years
guidance: CBT, mindfulness, and regular scheduled visits with a single physician to reduce unnecessary testing.
